Computational scientists and HPC engineers have always been among the earliest adopters of new computing paradigms, and agents are no exception. Today, research and engineering teams use AI models and agents for things such as ingesting dense scientific literature, optimizing code, and autonomously steering simulations.

Without deep infrastructure and domain context, an unguided agent can still pair incompatible storage tiers with compute-optimized VMs, overlook placement policies, or stall when diagnosing a multi-node MPI fabric error.

That challenge led our team to ask a simple question: What if we could package our deep HPC and scientific expertise into reusable agent skills, turning complex setup and optimization into guided workflows?

Synchronizing data between the two systems, often called Reverse ETL (Extract, Transform, Load), traditionally requires heavy middleware, staging buckets, and complex orchestration, especially at enterprise scale.

We’re announcing the general availability (GA) of BigQuery exports to AlloyDB, allowing data engineering teams to use a single, declarative SQL statement to export data from BigQuery to AlloyDB. This approach completely removes the need for complex ETL middleware.

Prolonged drought conditions affecting the Colorado River Basin led to record low hydropower generation this summer in the Southwestern electricity supply region, which includes Arizona, New Mexico, and small parts of Nevada and California. Hydropower generation from April through August 2026 was 19% lower than during the same period last year and 28% lower than the 10-year average, according to the latest data from our Form EIA-923 survey.

Water elevations at Lake Powell and Lake Mead, which are formed by the Glen Canyon Dam and Hoover Dam, respectively, hit record lows. To be able to generate hydropower at the Glen Canyon Dam, Lake Powell should have an elevation of at least 3,490 feet, also known as the minimum power pool. At the end of September, this elevation reached 3,518 feet, less than 1% above minimum power pool. The Hoover Dam requires an elevation of at least 950 feet at Lake Mead, which by the end of September reached 1,038 feet, 9% higher than minimum power pool. The U.S. Bureau of Reclamation manages most dams across the Colorado River Basin. Seven states (Arizona, California, Colorado, Nevada, New Mexico, Utah, and Wyoming) depend on the river for hydropower generation and for other water supply needs. Organization Policy Service can help you secure resource configurations and set up security guardrails across your Google Cloud resource hierarchy. Underwater forests of giant kelp protect coastlines, provide habitat, and support marine ecosystems — but they’re disappearing worldwide due to ocean warming. As COP31 kicks off this week, we’re sharing results from our partnership with Australia's national science agency, CSIRO, which is using AI and genomics to help restore giant kelp.

The team recently published two high-quality reference genomes for Australian giant kelp, providing a foundation for conservation genetics work. Next researchers trained a version of Google's open-source AI tool DeepVariant to analyze giant kelp DNA. It sequenced 600 wild specimens collected from 40 sites along the Tasmanian coast, where populations have dwindled to 5% of historic numbers.

This video explains how the genetic analysis and partners’ lab-based cross-breeding studies are laying the groundwork for a real-world outcome: giant kelp forests replanted with diverse, heat-tolerant specimens. This effort is part of Google Australia's Digital Futures Initiative.

items.title: Test your applications against AWS locally with AWS Emulator
items.summary: AWS Emulator is a free, open-source local emulator in Rust that lets developers test applications against nearly every AWS service on their own machine using the same CLI and SDK commands, with fidelity measured against real AWS behavior.
items.excerpt:
Today we’re announcing AWS Emulator, a local emulator for Amazon Web Services (AWS) that you run on your machine. The AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), the AWS SDKs, and your coding agents speak to it over a local HTTPS endpoint using the same AWS APIs they would use in the cloud, from your laptop. AWS Emulator has no additional service fee. You pay only for AWS resources when you deploy on AWS. Its source is on GitHub. You install it from an RPM or Debian package on Linux, and on macOS and Windows you run it in Docker.

How it works You install the emulator, start it, and point your tools at the local endpoint. When AWS Emulator starts, it generates its own credentials, a config file, and a certificate, and writes them to ~/.aws/emulator/9297/. You set environment variables so the AWS SDK talks to your laptop instead of AWS, and your application code stays unchanged.

From there, your existing tests, CLI scripts, and coding agents keep working the way they already do. A unit test that creates an Amazon DynamoDB table, writes an item, and reads it back is the same test, and it runs on your machine without a deployment. A coding agent can create resources, check the result, and iterate again without waiting on a deployment in a Region.

items.excerpt:
As the era of physical AI — in which AI systems perform physical tasks in the real world — takes shape, new standards are emerging for memory semiconductors. Robots and vehicles that make autonomous decisions and move independently can cause accidents if they malfunction or fall victim to data breaches. As a result, functional safety, which protects against unintended failures, and cybersecurity, which safeguards against malicious external attacks, have become essential requirements for memory.

Against this backdrop, SK hynix announced that its LPDDR5X* DRAM has obtained Safety Integrity Level 3 (SIL 3) certification under IEC 61508, the international standard for industrial functional safety, as well as Cybersecurity Management System (CSMS)* certification based on ISO/SAE 21434, the international standard for automotive cybersecurity. Both certifications were granted following rigorous assessments by the global certification body SGS-TÜV Saar (involving both SGS Korea and SGS Japan).

Building on its previously obtained ISO 26262 ASIL-D automotive functional safety certification, SK hynix has now extended its functional safety credentials beyond automotive applications to a broader range of industrial applications, including robotics and smart factories, while also validating its Cybersecurity Management System (CSMS) against international standards. To answer a complex business question, an AI agent must understand two things: what happened, and why. The what is a governed metric, like revenue at risk; the why is the network of relationships that produced it. Because metric definitions, a.k.a. measures, traditionally live in business intelligence (BI) platforms while relationships live in knowledge graphs, an AI agent only ever sees half the picture. It guesses the rest, leading to confident but sometimes wrong answers. To solve this hallucination problem, we introduced measures in BigQuery, which are now generally available.

Historically, organizations needing both BI and knowledge graphs had to run two siloed technology stacks: one to calculate reliable metrics, the other to map out entity relationships. Bridging them entailed brittle data pipelines and runtime reconciliation by analysts and AI agents, who held the connections in their heads or in sprawling prompts. This patchwork approach wasn't just slow and expensive — it’s where data governance broke down, as every analyst and prompt may define joins and metrics differently.

To replace manual reconciliation, you need a single model that understands both the structure of your business and the math that measures it. BigQuery measures builds directly on BigQuery Graph to deliver that unified foundation. Kubernetes, the open source system that manages how applications run across thousands of AI factories, has become the foundation for AI, and the demands on it are only growing.

To help meet them, NVIDIA is deepening its commitment to open source at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon, the flagship conference for the Kubernetes and cloud-native communities.

NVIDIA is contributing NVIDIA OpenShell, an open source runtime for securing and governing autonomous agents, to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF), a nonprofit that is part of the Linux Foundation and the host of KubeCon. As a CNCF Sandbox project, OpenShell will be governed by the organizations building it into their products and strengthened by the expertise of security professionals worldwide.

NVIDIA is also contributing to Agent Substrate, an open source Google-led framework for operating long-running agent workloads at scale on Kubernetes that has been accepted into the CNCF Sandbox.

Additionally, NVIDIA announced new components of the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform: NVIDIA Kubernetes Engine, NVIDIA Kubernetes Recipes and NVIDIA Snapshot. These tools help teams deploy, manage and scale GPU infrastructure on Kubernetes for AI factories.

Together, these advancements mark a step forward in making Kubernetes the leading foundation for AI workloads at scale — empowering developers to build safer, more efficient AI infrastructure for the future.

items.excerpt:
Standard Network Policies limit you to applying policies at the namespace level, but ClusterNetworkPolicy (CNP) lets you apply granular networking policies across an entire cluster. When you use CNP, you can easily scale security and governance policies. Recently, I experimented with this functionality in Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) and saw the benefits for myself.

In this post, we'll explore using CNP to control traffic to an LLM and cluster. If you want to jump right into a hands-on lab, check out this Codelab: Secure AI Inference Workloads with GKE ClusterNetworkPolicy.

CNP follows a three-tier flow with a precedence match:

Admin tier (top precedence): Cluster administrator enforces mandatory security rules that can't be bypassed (for example, blocking metadata access).

Network policy tier (middle precedence): Standard namespace-scoped policies that are managed by application teams to control ingress and egress for their microservices.

Baseline tier (bottom precedence): Cluster administrator establishes fallback defaults (for example, a default-deny posture across namespaces).

The aim of the experiment in the Codelab is to restrict traffic to the LLM namespace, allow only authorized clients, and prevent cluster-wide access to the metadata API except for DNS port 53. It uses these services:

Virtual Private Cloud (VPC): Provides private networking, subnets for pods and services, and secure outbound egress via Cloud NAT.
